# The Mobile Programmatic Ecosystem {.unnumbered}

Part I is a tour of how mobile ad tech works, before we build any models. It explains how a free game earns money from ads, how an advertiser buys new players through an auction that runs in a fraction of a second, how anyone knows whether an ad worked, and what happens inside the platform that does the bidding. It's written for data scientists and ML engineers who are new to ad tech, and it sets up the problems the rest of the book solves. There's no code in this part, and no math beyond a few multiplications, so it also works as an introduction for colleagues who don't build models.

We follow one story through all four chapters. Gem Garden, a free match-3 game, has an ad slot to fill. Cozy Farm Tycoon, a farming game, wants new players. In @sec-introduction, we meet the market they live in. In @sec-the-auction-lifecycle, an ad opportunity in Gem Garden turns into an auction and an impression. In @sec-measurement-and-mmps, a player taps the ad, installs Cozy Farm Tycoon, and makes a purchase. And in @sec-inside-a-demand-side-platform, we look at the DSP that bid on that impression, and end with the same bid worked out by the numbers.

A second thread runs through all four chapters. Mobile advertising is a crowded market, where many platforms compete to take credit for the same installs. A DSP that only collects credit is easy to replace. A DSP that causes installs that wouldn't have happened otherwise, and can prove it, is worth much more to an advertiser. We'll build up that case one chapter at a time.

If you already know how real-time bidding, MMPs, and DSPs work, feel free to skip ahead to Part II, where the hands-on work starts, and where the Gem Garden and Cozy Farm Tycoon story becomes something you can run on the book's companion bid simulator. The book is free online, so there's no cost to skimming. Two things from Part I are worth a look either way: the pricing vocabulary in @sec-inside-a-demand-side-platform, which the rest of the book uses, and the glossary in @sec-glossary.
